title: Hubble Interacting Galaxy NGC 6240
caption: Merging galaxy NGC 6240, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration, and A. Evans (University of Virginia, Charlottesville/NRAO/Stony Brook University)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: NGC 6240 has a peculiar shape that NASA likens to a butterfly or a lobster. It is the product of two smaller galaxies merging into one, and it lies some 400 million light-years away in Ophiuchus, the Serpent Holder.

The collision began about 30 million years ago. It set off a wave of star formation and touched off numerous supernova explosions. NASA expects the merger to finish within tens to hundreds of millions of years.

The galaxy also holds two giant black holes. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory found them in observations that put them about 3,000 light-years apart. Over time the pair is expected to drift toward each other and eventually combine into a single, larger black hole. Chandra detected them in X-rays, a kind of light Hubble's camera does not record.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys used a blue filter, F435W (B), and a near-infrared filter, F814W (I). NASA shows F435W in blue, F814W in red, and a combination of the two in green.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the black holes themselves were detected in X-rays, not in this image.

explore: Hubble's picture is part of a 2008 set of 59 merging-galaxy images released for the telescope's 18th launch anniversary. The galaxy is also listed as VV 617. Most of that anniversary set came from GOALS, a survey of luminous and ultra-luminous infrared galaxies.
alt: An irregular galaxy with a lobed, butterfly-like shape formed by two merging galaxies.
